questions.q: A read ACL exists on `task` requiring the `itil` role. No ACL exists directly on `problem`, but one exists directly on `incident` requiring `itil_admin`. What role does a user need to read a Problem record?
options: itil, inherited from the task-level ACL, since no more specific ACL exists for problem
itil_admin, inherited from the incident-level ACL
Both itil and itil_admin are required together
No role is required for Problem reads
questions.explain: Problem has no ACL of its own, so it falls back to the inherited task-level rule, which requires itil.

questions.q: Using the same setup, what role does a user need to read an Incident record, and why?
options: itil, because the task-level ACL always applies everywhere
itil_admin, because the more specific incident-level ACL overrides the inherited task-level one
Both itil and itil_admin, combined with AND
Whichever role has fewer permissions, since ACLs grant the narrower option
questions.explain: Most specific ACL wins: since incident has its own ACL for the read operation, it replaces the inherited task-level rule for Incident specifically.

questions.q: Look at this ACL script: `answer = gs.hasRole('itil') || current.caller_id == gs.getUserID();` defined on `incident` for the read operation. What does it mean for Problem and Change records?
options: It also governs Problem and Change, since they extend task the same way Incident does
It governs Incident only -- Problem and Change are unaffected by this ACL and use whatever ACL applies at their own level
It overrides every ACL on every table in the instance
It only runs if the task-level ACL is deleted first
questions.explain: An ACL defined directly on incident is scoped to incident. Problem and Change each resolve their own most-specific match independently.

questions.q: An admin changes the script on the task-level read ACL and then tests read access on an Incident record, expecting the behavior to change. Nothing changes. What is the most likely explanation?
options: ServiceNow caches ACL scripts for 24 hours before they take effect
Incident has its own, more specific read ACL, so it was never using the task-level ACL the admin edited
ACL scripts on task can never be edited after creation
The admin must also edit the ACL on problem for the change to take effect
questions.explain: This is the classic confusion the lesson calls out: Incident resolves to its own ACL first. Editing the inherited task-level rule has no visible effect on Incident if a more specific incident-level ACL exists.

questions.q: Before concluding an ACL "isn't working" on an extended table like Incident, what should an admin check in `sys_security_acl`?
options: Only the ACL on the exact table being tested -- the base table is irrelevant
Only the base-table ACL, since extended tables never have their own rules
Both the base-table ACL (table = task) and any ACL on the extended table (table = incident) for the same operation, to confirm which one is actually in effect
Nothing in sys_security_acl -- ACL behavior can only be diagnosed by trial and error
questions.explain: Because precedence resolves to the most specific match, diagnosing behavior correctly requires checking both levels, not assuming either one in isolation.
